answer.sourceLine: These are the opening words of 1 Timothy 6:10 in the King James Version ↗, where they read exactly as quoted. (The text reproduced there is the standard modern KJV — the 1769 Oxford revision, not the 1611 printing.) The letter names Paul as its author in its first verse — but most modern scholars hold that the Pastoral Epistles were written after his death ↗. So the sentence is certain; the hand that wrote it is not.

source.heading: The verse, and who wrote the letter

docMeta.dd: First Epistle of Paul the Apostle to Timothy (1 Timothy 6:10)
King James Version — 1769 Oxford text, as revised by Benjamin Blayney
Koine Greek — ῥίζα γὰρ πάντων τῶν κακῶν ἐστιν ἡ φιλαργυρία
Wording verified verbatim — authorship of the letter contested

source.excerpt: But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition. For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
trail: The verse reads verbatim in the Wikisource transcription of the King James text ↗, at chapter 6, verse 10.

It reads identically in Project Gutenberg’s King James Version of the Bible ↗, under the heading ‘The First Epistle of Paul the Apostle to Timothy’ — a second, independent transcription, so the wording does not rest on one editor.

A note on the edition, because it is easy to get wrong: the text linked above is not the 1611 printing. Wikisource’s King James Bible ↗ states in its own header that it reproduces ‘the 1769 King James Bible, as revised by Benjamin Blayney’ — the standardised text nearly every modern KJV descends from. The wording of this verse is the same; the spelling of the 1611 original is not.

On authorship, Wikipedia’s survey of the scholarship ↗ records that the letter names Paul at 1:1, that nineteenth- and twentieth-century scholarship questioned this, and that most scholars now hold the Pastorals to be by an unidentified writer of the late first to mid second century.
The Koine Greek behind the line — φιλαργυρία, philargyria, the love of silver — and William Tyndale’s earlier English rendering are both set out at Wikipedia’s article on the love of money ↗.
source.excerptNote: The quotation is the opening clause of verse 10, not a whole sentence. In the KJV the verse runs on past a colon to say what the love of money actually does — people “coveted after” it and so “erred from the faith”. Verse 9, printed here for context, is about the wanting, not the having.

author.name: Paul the Apostle
author.heading: About Paul the Apostle
author.metaLine: c. 5 – c. 64/65 AD · Apostle & letter-writer of the early Church
author.bio: Born Saul of Tarsus in Roman Cilicia around AD 5, Paul began as a persecutor of the first Christians and became the most prolific letter-writer of the early Church, founding congregations across Asia Minor and Europe from the mid-40s to the mid-50s AD. 1 Timothy is one of the three ‘Pastoral Epistles’ written in his name; unlike letters such as 1 Thessalonians or Romans, these are not generally accepted as his own work, and many scholars date them well after his death around AD 64–65.

misattribution.heading: The three words that go missing
misattribution.intro: The verse is quoted far more often in a shortened form, and the missing words carry the entire argument.

items.who: “Money is the root of all evil”
items.why: Drops the love of, and with it the subject of the sentence. The verse does not condemn money; it condemns wanting money, which is why verse 9 is about “they that will be rich” rather than they that are.

items.who: “For covetousness is the root of all evil”
items.why: William Tyndale rendered the same Greek this way ↗ — naming the vice outright rather than describing it, which makes plain that ‘money’ was never the thing being blamed.

items.who: “a root of all kinds of evil” (New International Version)
items.why: The same Wikipedia article ↗ notes the NIV’s wording and records that the grammarian Daniel B. Wallace lists six defensible translations of the Greek, because it is genuinely unclear whether ‘root’ is definite and whether ‘all’ means all without exclusion or all without distinction.

misattribution.truthLine: What the King James text actually says ↗ is “For the love of money is the root of all evil” — six words in, and the sentence has already told you the fault is in the appetite.

context.heading: Why ‘the love of’ is the whole sentence
lead: Shorten the verse and you get a line against money. Leave it whole and you get a line against a particular appetite — one that, on the letter’s own account, works by pulling people away from something they already had. The coin is neutral; the coveting is not.

That is why the shortened version is so much more quotable and so much less useful. “Money is the root of all evil” is a verdict on the world. “The love of money is the root of all evil” is a verdict on the reader.
context.detailsSummary: On the Greek, and the six ways to translate it
detailsBody: The Greek noun is philargyria (φιλαργυρία) — literally love-of-silver — and the clause reads, word for word, ‘for a root of all the evils is the love of money’.

Two ambiguities make the English genuinely hard: Greek has no indefinite article here, so ‘root’ may be a root or the root; and ‘all’ may mean all without exclusion or all without distinction. The KJV took the strong reading on both counts and the NIV the weak one, which is why the two English versions sound like different claims.
context.pull: The verse does not blame the coin. It blames the wanting.
